outline.description: Introduces large foundation models and motivates the need for efficient downstream adaptation. Provides a taxonomy of existing parameter-efficient fine‑tuning strategies and discusses their trade‑offs.
subtopics: The rise of large foundation models and their training costs
Why adapting pretrained models is essential
Model fine‑tuning versus adapters versus prompts
Desired properties for PEFT methods (parameter budget, inference latency, knowledge preservation)
High‑level contribution overview of the paper

outline.description: Explains why maintaining geometric relationships among neuron weight vectors is beneficial during adaptation. Introduces pairwise angles, orthogonal matrices, and their consequences for representation stability.
subtopics: Linear layers as sets of neuron vectors
Pairwise angular relationships and hyperspherical energy
Definition and key properties of orthogonal matrices
Multiplicative versus additive updates under geometric constraints
Prior work leveraging geometry in fine‑tuning

outline.description: Presents the original Orthogonal Fine‑tuning framework in detail—including mathematical formulation, Cayley parameterization, block‑diagonal variant—and analyzes its expressive power versus parameter cost.
subtopics: Formal definition of OFT: W' = R W⁰
Ensuring orthogonality during training via the Cayley transform
Block‑diagonal approximation: construction and parameter count
Empirical strengths of OFT (generalizability) versus its inefficiency
Motivating question: can a dense orthogonal matrix be trained efficiently?

outline.chapter_title: Information Transmission View on Sparse Orthogonal Factorizations
outline.description: Introduces a graph‑theoretic perspective that treats a product of sparse matrices as information flow across a layered grid graph. Establishes desiderata for constructing dense orthogonal transformations with few trainable edges.
subtopics: Motivation for an information transmission perspective
Mapping matrix products onto multi‑level graphs
Nodes, levels, edges: interpreting nonzero entries as communication links
(i) Dense connectivity requirement for full rank transformation
(ii) Minimal free edges under orthogonality constraints
Graphical comparison between block‑diagonal sparsity and potential alternatives

outline.chapter_title: Butterfly Structures in Fast Linear Transforms
outline.,description: Reviews the Cooley–Tukey FFT algorithm’s butterfly topology and shows how it yields sparse factorizations that achieve dense connectivity with only O(d log d) nonzero entries.
,subtopics: "Cooley–Tukey" recursive FFT algorithm fundamentals
"Butterfly" factor Bᴱ(k): definition and parametric form
"Recursive construction" of the full d‑dimensional butterfly matrix B(d)
"Butterfly graphs" visualized as edge patterns across levels
"Block‑butterfly" components \tilde{B}ᵇ(d,k) for arbitrary block size b
"Ensuring orthogonality" within each sparse factor via small rotations or Cayley parametrization
"Parameter complexity analysis" leading to O(d log d)

outline.chapter_title: Orthogonal Butterfly Fine‑tuning (BOFT): Architecture and Parameters
outline.,description: Describes how BOFT composes multiple orthogonal butterfly components into a trainable transformation R(m,b). Covers hyperparameters m (number of factors) and b (block size), special cases linking back to OFT, identity initialization strategy, multiplicative dropout design, and algorithmic workflow.
,subtopics: "Formulation" R(m,b)=∏_{i=1}^{m}\tilde{B}^{b}_{(d,i)}
"Hyperparameter trade‑off": number of factors vs block size
"Special cases": BOFT(1,b) → block‑diagonal OFT; BOFT(log₂d ,2) → dense orthogonal matrix with O(d log d) parameters;
"Parameter count derivation": \frac{1}{2}(b−1)d m
"Identity initialization" using zero skew-symmetric matrices in the Cayley transform
"Multiplicative dropout": random masking at factor level p₁ and at internal block level p₂
"Forward pass integration" within transformer linear layers or diffusion model UNets
"Pseudo-code summary"

outline.chapter_title: Theoretical Insights into BOFA’s Expressivity and Stability
outline.,description: Provides rigorous analysis showing that BOFT is strictly more expressive than block-diagonal OFT while preserving spectral properties. Includes theorem statements, proof sketches, approximation experiments versus random orthogonal matrices, connections to bilinear similarity learning.
,subtopics: "Expressivity theorem": composition of butterfly matrices can approximate any d×d orthogonal matrix
"Intuition behind universal approximation": permutations + small rotations
"Simulation study": error vs effective trainable parameters when approximating random orthogonal matrices
"Spectral norm preservation": proof via singular value decomposition
"Relation to bilinear similarity/metric learning": learning R under orthogonality constraints
"Inductive bias discussion": why structured subsets improve generalisation

outline.,description: Details practical aspects such as optimizer choice, learning-rate schedules compatible with low‑discrepancy updates, gradient handling through the Cayley parametrization, efficient implementation of multiple sparse multiplications, hyperparameter tuning guidelines for m/b/p₁/p₂,and runtime overhead mitigation.
,subtopics: "Optimizer selection"—AdamW vs SGD with small LR
"Gradient flow through Cayley transform"—maintaining skew symmetry
"Efficient computation"—batching sparse–dense multiplications
"Hyperparameter tuning"—recommended ranges for m,b based on model dimension
"Multiplicative dropout configuration"—choosing p₁,p₂ empirically
"Training runtime analysis" compared against vanilla OFT/LORA
"Post-finetune merging"—absorbing learned R into frozen weights at inference time

outline.,chapter_title: Empirical Evaluation Across Vision-, Language-, And Diffusion Tasks
outline.,description: Presents extensive experimental results demonstrating BOFT’s superiority over state-of-the-art PEFT methods on large vision transformers, large language models,and text-to-image diffusion models.
,subtopics: "Benchmark suite overview": datasets/tasks per modality (ImageNet/VTAB+, GLUE/SuperGLUE/T0?, Stable Diffusion controllability)
"Baseline portfolio": full fine‑tune、LoRA、BitFit、Adapter、Prompt tuning
"Vision transformer results": accuracy gains under identical parameter budgets
"Large language model results": perplexity/F1 improvements
"Diffusion model control experiments": qualitative & quantitative gains
"Ablation studies": impact of varying m , b , dropout probabilities
"Interpolation experiment": smooth transition from identity → learned R visualized
"Summary tables": parameter budget vs performance trade-offs

outline.,chapter_title: Practical Deployment Guidelines And Future Directions
outline.,description: Summarizes best practices when applying BOFT in real-world pipelines—including hyperparameter selection under resource constraints—and discusses current limitations along with promising research avenues such as alternative sparsity topologies or hybrid low-rank/butterfly schemes.
,subtopics: "Choosing m/b for production constraints"—memory vs computation considerations
"End-to-end fine‑tune workflow"—checkpoint handling , logging , monitoring
"Merging steps at inference"—zero-latency deployment after training
"Limitations highlighted by authors"—training runtime overhead , reliance on FFT-inspired topology
"Beyond butterflies": other network topologies from computer networking that may yield better edge efficiency
"Hybrid approaches"—combining low-rank LoRA style updates with butterfly priors
"Open research questions"
